posts.title: Agent evals in 400 lines
posts.hook: Lilian Weng's team open-sourced their agent eval harness. 400 lines of Python. Six months of internal work.
posts.body:
Lilian Weng's team open-sourced their agent eval harness. 400 lines of Python. Six months of internal work.

I've been building agent workflows for GTM for over a year now and the eval problem is the one nobody wants to talk about.

You ship an enrichment agent that pulls company data from 4 sources, scores it, and writes to your CRM. It works Tuesday. Wednesday someone changes an API response shape and your agent hallucinates a revenue number. Nobody catches it for two weeks.

The pattern I've landed on is dead simple. Golden input/output pairs stored in a JSON file. Run the agent, diff the output, flag drift above a threshold. It's not fancy. It catches 80% of the silent failures that actually cost you pipeline.

What's interesting about Weng's harness is they measure tool-call sequences, not just final output. That matters. An agent can get the right answer through a completely wrong path, and that wrong path will break on the next edge case.

If you're building agents for anything beyond demos, the eval layer isn't optional. It's the difference between a prototype and something you can actually trust with production data.

The 400-line version is a good starting point. Most teams need less, not more.

remixes.label: tactical-breakdown
remixes.hook: The hardest part of running AI agents isn't building them. It's knowing when they break.
remixes.body:
The hardest part of running AI agents isn't building them. It's knowing when they break.

Lilian Weng's team just dropped their internal agent eval harness as open source. 400 lines of Python. And it crystallized something I've been struggling with for months.

When I build an enrichment pipeline for a client, the demo always works. Pull company data, score it, push to CRM. Beautiful. But production is a different animal.

APIs change response formats without warning. A data provider starts returning nulls for a field you depend on. Your scoring logic drifts because the training distribution shifted. And you don't find out until someone on the sales team asks why half their leads have no revenue data.

The eval problem breaks down into three parts. First, defining what "correct" even means for non-deterministic outputs. Second, catching regressions before they hit your pipeline. Third, doing this without spending more engineering time on evals than on the agent itself.

What I've landed on is dead simple. Golden datasets with known-good outputs. Run them on every deploy. Compare against a similarity threshold, not exact match. Alert on drift.

It's not sophisticated. But it catches 80% of the breaks before they reach production.
remixes.cta: What's your threshold for "good enough" when evaluating agent outputs? The exact-match crowd and the vibes-based crowd seem to live on different planets.

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: Most teams evaluating their AI agents are measuring the wrong thing entirely.
remixes.body:
Most teams evaluating their AI agents are measuring the wrong thing entirely.

They measure accuracy. Did the agent return the right answer? But in production GTM workflows, accuracy is table stakes. The question that actually matters is: did the agent fail gracefully when it couldn't get the right answer?

Lilian Weng's team open-sourced their eval harness this week. 400 lines. Worth reading not for the code but for the philosophy. They're testing behavior patterns, not just outputs.

I learned this the hard way running enrichment agents. My agent was 94% accurate on company data pulls. Looked great in the dashboard. But that 6% failure rate was silent. No errors, no alerts. Just bad data flowing into Attio, poisoning lead scores, wasting rep time on dead accounts.

The fix wasn't making the agent more accurate. It was making it louder when it wasn't confident. Adding uncertainty flags. Routing low-confidence results to a human review queue instead of auto-writing to CRM.

Eval isn't about proving your agent works. It's about proving you'll know when it doesn't.
remixes.cta: How do you handle the confidence gap? Agents that are right 90% of the time but can't tell you which 10% they got wrong.

posts.title: CRM is lying to leadership
posts.hook: Your CRM win rate is probably wrong by 15-20 points.
posts.body:
Your CRM win rate is probably wrong by 15-20 points.

I see this constantly building GTM systems for companies. They pull a win rate from Salesforce, present it to the board, and it looks healthy. But nobody scrubbed the denominator.

Dead opps sitting in Stage 2 for 90 days. Duplicates from the SDR team creating new records instead of updating existing ones. "Closed Lost" reasons that are blank because reps skip the field. Partner deals counted as outbound wins.

I built a pipeline audit script last month. 47 lines of Python, hits the CRM API, flags opps that haven't had activity in 2x the average stage duration. First client I ran it on... 38% of their "active pipeline" was dead weight. Their real win rate dropped from 28% to 19%.

The fix isn't a new tool. It's a weekly hygiene pass. Query opps with no activity past threshold, force a disposition, and actually close the ones that are done.

Leadership makes resource decisions based on these numbers. Hiring plans. Territory assignments. Quota setting. When the data is off by 15 points, every downstream decision is wrong too.

The script isn't complicated. The discipline to run it every week is the hard part.
posts.cta: Anyone else running automated pipeline hygiene? Would share the script if there's interest.

remixes.label: forensic-audit
remixes.hook: I audited a Series B company's pipeline last month. Their reported win rate was 34%. The real number was 19%.
remixes.body:
I audited a Series B company's pipeline last month. Their reported win rate was 34%. The real number was 19%.

The gap wasn't fraud. It was hygiene. And it's everywhere.

Here's what I found when I actually looked at the data. 47 opportunities stuck in Stage 2 for over 90 days. Still "open" in the system. Still counted in the denominator. Another 23 that were duplicates created by SDRs who couldn't find the existing record so they made a new one. And 31 marked "Closed Lost" with no reason attached, which means nobody actually confirmed they were lost.

When you clean all that up, the win rate drops by 15 points. The pipeline coverage ratio drops with it. And suddenly that board slide telling everyone the GTM motion is working looks very different.

The fix isn't complicated. I run a weekly script that flags stale opps, catches duplicates by domain matching, and forces a disposition on anything that's been untouched for 30 days. Takes maybe 200 lines of Python and a Slack webhook.

But the organizational fix is harder. Someone has to want accurate numbers more than they want comfortable ones.
remixes.cta: What's the most misleading metric you've seen presented to leadership with a straight face?

remixes.label: systems-thinking
remixes.hook: CRM data quality isn't an ops problem. It's a leadership problem wearing an ops costume.
remixes.body:
CRM data quality isn't an ops problem. It's a leadership problem wearing an ops costume.

Every RevOps person I talk to knows their pipeline data is dirty. They know the win rate is inflated. They know there are ghost opportunities sitting in Stage 1 from six months ago. They know the "Closed Lost" reasons are mostly blank.

They also know that cleaning it up means the numbers go down. And when the numbers go down, someone asks uncomfortable questions.

So the data stays dirty. And every decision built on that data carries a 15-20 point margin of error that nobody acknowledges.

I've built automated pipeline hygiene systems for GTM teams and the technical part is straightforward. Flag opps with no activity for 30+ days. Deduplicate by domain. Require disposition reasons. Auto-archive stale pipeline. Run it weekly.

The hard part is the conversation that happens when you turn it on. "Why did our pipeline drop 40% overnight?" It didn't drop. You're just seeing it accurately for the first time.

The companies that get through that conversation and keep the hygiene running are the ones that start making real decisions instead of comfortable ones.

posts.title: 72-hour ship vs 3-month build
posts.hook: Saw Priya Nair ship a working product in 72 hours with Claude Code. That tracks with what I'm seeing.
posts.body:
Saw Priya Nair ship a working product in 72 hours with Claude Code. That tracks with what I'm seeing.

I built Clearbox's first working version in a weekend. Reddit intent monitoring, scoring engine, Attio integration. Not a landing page. A working product processing real data.

Three years ago that's a 2-month sprint with a small team.

But here's what nobody talks about after the 72-hour build. The next 6 weeks are where it gets real. Edge cases in the data pipeline. The scoring model drifting because Reddit changed their API response. Users wanting filters you didn't think of.

The coding agent gets you to "it works" fast. Staying at "it works reliably" is still a grind.

What actually changed is the cost of trying. I can test 3 product ideas in the time it used to take to spec one. Most of them don't work. That's fine. The ones that do have real usage data behind them, not just a pitch deck.

The shift isn't "AI builds your product." It's that experimentation got cheap enough to run like a portfolio. Ship fast, measure, kill or keep. The build isn't the bottleneck anymore. Taste is.
posts.cta: What's your ratio of things shipped to things that actually stuck?

remixes.label: survival-rate
remixes.hook: I've shipped 14 tools in the last year. Three are still running. That ratio is the actual story.
remixes.body:
I've shipped 14 tools in the last year. Three are still running. That ratio is the actual story.

Everyone celebrates the 72-hour build. Priya Nair shipped a working product in a weekend with Claude Code. I built Clearbox's first version in similar time. Reddit monitoring, scoring engine, CRM integration. Real data flowing through a real pipeline.

The speed is real. I'm not disputing that. What I am saying is that shipping speed and survival rate are completely different metrics, and we're only celebrating one of them.

Of those 14 tools I built, the ones that died fell into three categories. First, things I built before I understood the actual user need. Fast to build, fast to abandon. Second, things that worked in isolation but couldn't integrate with the existing workflow. Third, things that required ongoing maintenance I didn't budget for.

The three that survived had something in common. I built them because someone was already doing the job manually and hating it. The tool replaced a specific, painful, repeated action. Not a hypothetical one.

The 72-hour build is the beginning of the story. The 90-day survival check is where the story actually gets interesting.

Speed to ship is a solved problem now. Speed to product-market fit is not.
remixes.cta: What's the survival rate on things you've shipped fast? Genuinely curious if the 3-out-of-14 ratio is normal or if I'm just bad at picking what to build.

remixes.label: hidden-cost
remixes.hook: The 72-hour build has a hidden cost nobody puts in the launch tweet.
remixes.body:
The 72-hour build has a hidden cost nobody puts in the launch tweet.

I watched Priya Nair ship a working product in 72 hours with Claude Code. Impressive and legitimate. I did something similar with Clearbox. Reddit intent monitoring, scoring, Attio integration. Weekend build. Real data.

But here's what happened in the weeks after. Edge cases surfaced that took longer to fix than the original build. Users did things I didn't anticipate. An API I depended on changed rate limits. The scoring logic needed tuning because real-world data distribution didn't match my test set.

None of this is a criticism of fast building. It's an observation that the build is maybe 20% of the total effort. The other 80% is the unglamorous work of making it reliable, maintaining it, and iterating based on actual usage.

Three years ago, a 2-month sprint with a team handled both the build and the hardening in one pass. Now we compress the build to 72 hours but the hardening still takes weeks. We didn't eliminate the work. We front-loaded the dopamine.

The founders I see winning aren't the fastest shippers. They're the ones who ship fast and then stay long enough to do the boring part.

posts.title: Distribution over creation
posts.hook: We have a content creation problem the same way we have a food production problem. We don't. We have a distribution problem.
posts.body:
We have a content creation problem the same way we have a food production problem. We don't. We have a distribution problem.

I can generate 10 LinkedIn posts, 3 Reddit threads, an X thread, and a newsletter in a single Claude Code session. The creation part is solved. What's not solved is getting the right piece in front of the right person at the right time.

The content stack I actually use now looks nothing like what "content strategy" decks recommend.

✅ Write one deep piece per week (blog or newsletter)
✅ Repurpose into platform-native formats (not cross-post, actually rewrite)
✅ Scout Reddit and X for conversations where the piece is genuinely relevant
✅ Drop it in context, not as a link dump

The third step is where 90% of content programs fail. They publish and pray. Or they spam the same link to 5 platforms with identical copy.

Distribution is a research problem. You need to know where your audience actually talks, what language they use, and what questions they're already asking. Then you show up with something useful.

I built a Reddit scout that monitors 12 subreddits for intent signals. Not keyword matches. Actual buying intent patterns. That single script drives more qualified conversations than any amount of content volume ever did.
posts.cta: What's your distribution setup look like right now? Curious where people are seeing actual traction.

inspired_by.summary: Content strategy in 2026 is a distribution problem, not a creation problem. We have more content than ever and less organic reach than ever. The brands winning right now have one thing in common: they treat LinkedIn as the top of a conversion funnel with a clear next step, not a broadcast channel. Here's the 3-part framework we use for every client to turn posts into pipeline.

remixes.label: distribution-stack
remixes.hook: I generate 15+ pieces of content per week. My distribution system is the only reason any of it works.
remixes.body:
I generate 15+ pieces of content per week. My distribution system is the only reason any of it works.

Creation is solved. I'm not being hyperbolic. In a single Claude Code session I can produce LinkedIn posts, Reddit threads, X threads, and a newsletter draft. The raw material is abundant.

But abundant content without targeted distribution is just noise. And most people I talk to are still in the "post and pray" phase. Write something, put it on LinkedIn, hope the algorithm is kind.

Here's what actually moves the needle. Platform-native adaptation, not cross-posting. The same insight needs a different shape for Reddit than LinkedIn than X. Reddit wants context and technical depth. LinkedIn wants a hook and a professional angle. X wants compression and edge.

Timing and sequencing matter more than volume. I test hooks on X first because feedback is fastest. Winners get expanded into LinkedIn posts. The best performers become newsletter deep-dives. Losers get killed before I invest more time.

Channel selection based on where the audience already is. I found my best engagement on Reddit in niche subreddits with 5-15K members. Not on LinkedIn with its 900M users.

The content itself is the cheapest part of the stack now. The distribution logic is where the leverage lives.
remixes.cta: What's your highest-ROI distribution channel right now? Not where you post the most, where you get the most actual results.

remixes.hook: Stop creating content. You already have too much. Start distributing what you have.
remixes.body:
Stop creating content. You already have too much. Start distributing what you have.

I spent three months this year in pure creation mode. Multiple posts per day across platforms. Threads, newsletters, comments. Volume was through the roof.

Engagement was flat. Pipeline impact was negligible.

Then I flipped the ratio. Instead of 80% creation and 20% distribution, I went 30% creation and 70% distribution. Fewer new pieces. Way more time spent getting existing pieces in front of the right people.

What that looks like in practice. Taking a LinkedIn post that performed well and reworking it as a Reddit thread in a specific subreddit. Finding conversations where my existing content directly answers someone's question. Repurposing newsletter content into targeted comments on other people's posts.

The insight is uncomfortable for people who love creating. Your best post from last month, the one that got 200 likes, probably reached 3% of the people who would find it valuable. The other 97% never saw it. And instead of solving that distribution gap, you wrote 15 new posts.

We have a content creation problem the same way we have a food production problem. We don't. We have a distribution problem. And AI makes the imbalance worse because it makes creation even cheaper.

posts.title: Stack collapse to three layers
posts.hook: The AI infrastructure stack is collapsing into three layers: model, orchestration, memory. Everything else is getting absorbed.
posts.body:
The AI infrastructure stack is collapsing into three layers: model, orchestration, memory. Everything else is getting absorbed.

I'm watching this happen in real time in GTM.

Two years ago you needed Clay for enrichment, Apollo for contact data, Lemlist for sequencing, Salesforce for CRM, Gong for call intel, 6sense for intent. Each tool owned a layer.

Now I run enrichment through API calls in a Python script. Sequencing through Lemlist's API. CRM in Attio. Intent monitoring with a custom Reddit/X scraper. The orchestration layer is Claude Code.

The tools didn't disappear. They became APIs I call from one orchestration layer instead of 8 browser tabs I context-switch between.

Memory is the interesting one. Right now I use SQLite files and JSON. But the teams building proper agent memory... vector stores with temporal awareness, conversation history that persists across sessions, knowledge graphs that update themselves... that layer is going to matter more than the model layer within 18 months.

The model is becoming commodity. Orchestration is where the workflow logic lives. Memory is where the compounding advantage builds.

If you're buying point tools in 2026, ask which layer they actually own. Most of them are just thin wrappers around the orchestration layer, and that's exactly what agents replace first.

I replaced 6 GTM tools with API calls inside a Claude Code project. The stack isn't shrinking. It already shrank.

Two years ago my GTM stack looked like everyone else's. Clay for enrichment. Apollo for contact data. Lemlist for sequences. Attio for CRM. Various tools for intent signals. Each with its own login, its own pricing tier, its own data format.

Today I run enrichment through direct API calls. Contact data comes from providers I hit programmatically. Sequencing is orchestrated in code. The CRM is still Attio because I need a UI for the sales team, but even that is mostly written to via API.

What changed isn't that better tools appeared. What changed is that the orchestration layer got powerful enough to absorb the features that used to justify standalone products.

When your orchestration layer can call any API, transform any data, and maintain state across runs, most SaaS tools become expensive wrappers around API calls you could make yourself.

The three layers that remain: the model (reasoning), orchestration (the code that ties it together), and memory (the data and context that persists). Everything else is a convenience tax.

I'm not saying every company should rip out their stack tomorrow. If you don't have someone who can write and maintain the orchestration code, the tools still provide value. But the ceiling on that value is dropping fast.

Three layers. Model, orchestration, memory. Everything else is negotiable.

posts.title: From plumber to builder pattern
posts.hook: HVAC contractors and plumbing shops are one of the most underserved B2B SaaS markets. I would know.
posts.body:
HVAC contractors and plumbing shops are one of the most underserved B2B SaaS markets. I would know.

Tom Brecker posted about failing at three SaaS ideas before finding traction with an HVAC niche tool. That resonated. I was a plumber for 10 years before I got into tech, and the software trades companies use is either ancient or built by people who've never set foot on a job site.

The scheduling tools don't account for drive time between jobs. The CRMs don't track which tech is certified for which equipment type. The estimating software doesn't pull from actual supplier pricing APIs.

Every single one of these is a solvable problem with a coding agent and a weekend.

The advantage Tom has, and that anyone with domain experience has, is knowing which problem actually matters. Generic SaaS founders build features. Domain experts build workflows that match how the work actually happens.

I think the next wave of successful solo founders won't be developers who learn a market. They'll be domain experts who learn to prompt. A plumber who can describe their dispatch workflow to Claude Code is closer to a working product than a developer who's never dispatched a service call.

The barrier to entry just moved from "can you code" to "do you understand the problem."

Trades software is a $14B market dominated by products that feel like they were designed in 2009 and never updated. The UX assumes office workers, not field techs with wet hands and 10 minutes between jobs.

The moat isn't technical. It's empathy. When you've done the work, you know which features are vanity and which ones save a crew 45 minutes a day. You know that a dispatcher doesn't need a dashboard. They need a single screen that answers one question: who's closest and available.

Domain expertise isn't a nice-to-have in vertical SaaS. It's the entire product strategy.

Horizontal SaaS is a bloodbath. Vertical SaaS for trades is a gold mine with almost no competition.

There are 3.5 million trade businesses in the US. Plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing. Most of them run on a combination of QuickBooks, a shared Google Calendar, and text messages. That's the tech stack for companies doing $2M to $15M in revenue.

Tom Brecker tried building broad tools three times and failed. His fourth attempt targeted HVAC shops specifically. It worked because he stopped trying to serve everyone and started solving one crew's Tuesday morning.

I was a plumber for a decade. The software problem isn't that it doesn't exist. It's that existing tools were built top-down by people who've never dispatched a truck or dealt with a no-show on a service call. They add features for enterprise. Meanwhile, a 12-person plumbing company needs three things: schedule jobs, track parts, send invoices. That's it.

The founders winning in vertical SaaS right now aren't the ones with the best engineering teams. They're the ones who used to BE the customer.

Niche selection isn't market research. It's autobiography.

posts.title: SDR research time isn't the bottleneck
posts.hook: Vin Matano cut SDR research time by 73% with Claude + Clay + Lemlist. Good result, but I think the metric is wrong.
posts.body:
Vin Matano cut SDR research time by 73% with Claude + Clay + Lemlist. Good result, but I think the metric is wrong.

Research time was never the real bottleneck. Relevance was.

An SDR can research a prospect in 4 minutes or 40 minutes. If the prospect isn't in-market, both are wasted. The 73% time savings means you burn through bad prospects faster. That's an improvement but it's optimizing the wrong layer.

The stack I'm building flips the sequence.

1. Monitor intent signals first (Reddit posts, job listings, tech stack changes, funding rounds)
2. Only research prospects who already showed a signal
3. Enrich with context from the signal itself, not generic company data

When you lead with intent, research time drops AND relevance goes up. You're not asking "what can I learn about this company." You're asking "they just posted about this specific problem, what's the angle."

The difference in reply rates is significant. Generic personalized outbound ("I saw you're hiring for X") gets 2-4%. Signal-led outbound ("you posted about Y problem, here's how we solved it") gets 8-12% in my data.

AI makes research faster. Intent makes research unnecessary for the 80% of prospects who aren't ready.

remixes.label: signal-before-speed
remixes.hook: SDR teams are celebrating doing the wrong work faster. That's not a win.
remixes.body:
SDR teams are celebrating doing the wrong work faster. That's not a win.

Vin Matano shared how he cut research time by 73% using Claude, Clay, and Lemlist. Impressive engineering. But it raises a question nobody's asking: what if the research itself isn't the problem?

Here's what I see in the outbound pipelines I build. The average SDR spends 60% of their time researching accounts that will never buy. Not because the research is bad. Because the accounts aren't in-market. No hiring signals. No tech changes. No budget triggers. Just names on a list that fit a firmographic filter.

Cutting research time from 12 minutes to 3 minutes per prospect means you can reach 4x more prospects. But if 80% of them are out-of-market, you just quadrupled your spam output.

The better stack flips the sequence. Signal detection first. Research second. You monitor job posts, technology installs, funding rounds, and community activity. When an account lights up across two or more signals, THEN you research them.

The result isn't faster research. It's fewer prospects who get researched, but every one of them is worth the conversation.

Speed without targeting is just organized waste.
remixes.cta: What signal combination gives you the most confidence that an account is actually ready to buy?

remixes.label: relevance-gap
remixes.hook: AI made outbound 4x faster. Reply rates stayed flat. That tells you everything.
remixes.body:
AI made outbound 4x faster. Reply rates stayed flat. That tells you everything.

Vin Matano's setup with Claude, Clay, and Lemlist cut SDR research time by 73%. Real result, solid tooling. But I keep seeing the same pattern across teams that adopt these stacks: throughput goes up, conversion doesn't.

The problem is sequence. Most outbound workflows go: build list, research list, write emails, send. AI accelerates steps 2 and 3. But step 1 is where the waste happens. If 60% of your list was never going to be in-market, you've automated the process of sending better-written emails to the wrong people.

I've been building intent-first pipelines at Clearbox for months now. The architecture is simple. Layer 1: passive signal collection. Job posts, tech stack changes, funding events, community mentions. Layer 2: signal scoring. One signal is noise. Two is a pattern. Three is a buying committee in motion. Layer 3: research only the accounts that pass scoring.

This inverts the funnel. Instead of researching 200 accounts and finding 30 worth emailing, you monitor 2,000 accounts passively and research the 40 that are actually moving.

The ROI isn't in faster research. It's in knowing who to research at all.

posts.title: Claude Code replaced Stack Overflow
posts.hook: 68% of senior engineers say Claude Code replaced Stack Overflow. The other 32% are probably lying.
posts.body:
68% of senior engineers say Claude Code replaced Stack Overflow. The other 32% are probably lying.

Gergely Orosz's survey of 1,200 engineers surfaced what everyone already feels. The search-copy-adapt loop from Stack Overflow is slower than telling Claude Code what you want and watching it write the implementation.

But the nuance matters. Claude Code didn't replace the knowledge that Stack Overflow represented. It replaced the retrieval mechanism.

I still need to understand what a webhook handler should do. I still need to know that SQLite has write concurrency limits. I still need to catch when the agent writes an N+1 query. The knowledge floor didn't drop. The speed ceiling went up.

What I've noticed in my own workflow... I'm a better reviewer than I was a writer. I can evaluate 10 approaches from Claude Code faster than I could write 1 approach from scratch. The skill shifted from "can you write this" to "can you tell whether this is correct."

That's a different muscle. And it's one that junior developers haven't built yet because they skipped the part where you debug your own bad code for 3 years.

The tool changed. The required judgment didn't.

The engineers who thrive with AI tools will be the ones who still insist on understanding the code they ship. Not because it's noble. Because when Claude generates something subtly wrong, understanding is the only thing that catches it.

Speed without comprehension is technical debt with a longer fuse.

posts.title: Pipeline coverage math is broken
posts.hook: 3x pipeline coverage used to mean something. Now it's a vanity metric most teams use to feel safe.
posts.body:
3x pipeline coverage used to mean something. Now it's a vanity metric most teams use to feel safe.

Kyle Coleman nailed this. Companies count everything in Stage 2+ as coverage, but 60% of it will never close. So your "3x coverage" is actually 1.2x of real pipeline. And 1.2x means you're going to miss.

I built a weighted pipeline model for a client last quarter. Simple logic.

✅ Stage 2 opps with no next step scheduled --> 20% weight
✅ Stage 3 opps past average stage duration --> 40% weight
✅ Stage 3 opps with recent activity and next step --> 80% weight
✅ Stage 4+ with verbal commit --> 90% weight

Same pipeline, same total dollar value. Weighted coverage dropped from 3.2x to 1.8x. The CEO's face when we showed that slide was... educational.

The weighted model forced honest conversations. Two reps had inflated pipelines they'd been rolling forward for quarters. Three opps were double-counted across territories. One "Stage 4" deal hadn't had a meeting in 45 days.

Clean math changes behavior. When reps know dead weight hurts their coverage number, they either work the deal or close it out. Both are better than pretending.

47 lines of Python against the CRM API. That's all it took.

Kyle Coleman made a sharp point about pipeline coverage math that most rev teams are still ignoring. The standard calculation counts everything in Stage 2 and above as coverage. But not all pipeline is equal, and pretending it is will make you miss your number.

I built a weighted model for a client last quarter that exposed the gap. Here's the simplified version.

Stage 2 opportunities with no champion identified: weighted at 10%. Stage 3 with a champion but no technical validation: 30%. Stage 4 with completed eval and procurement engaged: 70%. Anything past Stage 5 with a verbal commit: 85%.

Their raw pipeline said 3.2x coverage. The weighted model said 1.4x. They adjusted their outbound targets the next week.

The problem with flat coverage math is that it treats a first-meeting deal the same as a deal in procurement review. Your board sees 3x and feels comfortable. Your rep who knows which deals are real sees the gap but can't articulate it in a way that changes behavior.

Weighted coverage isn't complicated to build. Pull your historical close rates by stage. Apply those rates as multipliers. The number you get back is closer to reality than anything in your forecast slide.

Stop counting pipeline. Start weighing it.

The first month, their reported pipeline dropped by 40%. The second month, their forecast accuracy went from 62% to 84%. They didn't add any new pipeline. They just stopped lying about the pipeline they had.

Accurate pipeline is smaller pipeline. That's the part nobody wants to accept.

posts.title: Zero marketing budget to 10k MRR
posts.hook: Maya Chen hit $10k MRR with zero marketing budget. The playbook is simpler than people want it to be.
posts.body:
Maya Chen hit $10k MRR with zero marketing budget. The playbook is simpler than people want it to be.

Ship fast. Talk to users. Repeat.

I've been running Clearbox the same way. No paid ads. No content team. No marketing automation platform. Just building in public, showing up in communities where my buyers hang out, and having real conversations about the problem I'm solving.

The "zero marketing budget" framing is slightly misleading though. Time is a budget. I spend 5-6 hours a week on Reddit, LinkedIn, and X. Not posting content. Having conversations. Answering questions. Sharing what I'm building and what I'm learning.

That's not zero cost. It's sweat equity in distribution.

The pattern I see across every solo founder hitting early traction without paid:

1. They're in the community before they have something to sell
2. They share process, not just results
3. They respond to every comment and DM
4. They build the thing people in the community are asking for

Paid acquisition works when you've already proven the message converts organically. Running ads before you have organic signal is like warming up a domain you've never sent from. You're spending money to learn something you could learn for free.

Organic first. Paid to scale what already works.
